opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the core practical problems in what we call AI control. The basic situation is this: once you have AI agents doing large amounts of real work inside an AI company, writing code, running experiments, touching infrastructure, you might have millions of actions per day. Some small fraction of those will look somewhat suspicious. Almost all of the suspicious-looking ones will be innocent: the model was confused, or the task required something that superficially resembles an attack. But you're worried that a tiny number might be a scheming model actually trying to do something bad, like exfiltrate its weights or sabotage safety research.

You obviously can't have humans look carefully at everything. So the way I think about it is as a pipeline with a limited budget at each stage.

At the bottom you have cheap automated monitoring. You run a trusted model, something weaker that you're confident isn't colluding, over every action and have it produce a suspicion score. You might also use the untrusted model itself as a monitor, with tricks to make collusion harder, like paraphrasing inputs or testing it on fake attacks we've constructed to check that it reports them.

Then you escalate. The top fraction of a percent by suspicion gets more expensive scrutiny: more compute, more careful model-based analysis, maybe resampling. You ask the agent to redo the step a few times and see whether it keeps reaching for the weird thing. That turns out to be informative. An innocent model that did something odd once usually won't do it again, while a model that's actually trying to accomplish something has to keep trying.

Only at the very top do humans get involved, and you want to make their time count. You don't just hand an auditor a raw transcript and say "is this bad?" You give them tooling: what the action actually does, what files it touches, what the model was asked to do, similar past actions. Ideally the investigator can interactively probe the situation, rerunning the agent in a sandbox, varying the context, checking whether the behavior is robust.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that the goal of investigation shifts depending on what you find. Most of the time you're trying to quickly clear false positives so you don't drown. But if you find something that genuinely looks like an intentional attack, that's enormously valuable. It's the kind of evidence that might change how the company or the world treats these models. So you want a process designed both to block bad actions in the moment and to build a really compelling case when you catch something. Those are different jobs, and I think people underrate the second one.

Finally, a lot of this comes down to deciding up front which actions you can afford to let run while they're being reviewed and which ones need to block until someone has looked. For low-stakes stuff you can audit asynchronously after the fact. For things that are irreversible, like touching model weights or changing security permissions, you want them held until they've cleared review. Getting that categorization right is a big part of making the whole thing affordable.

r001.rationale: The response proposes scoring every action with a trusted automated monitor, then sending only the top fraction by suspicion to more expensive scrutiny.

r002.rationale: It says humans get involved only at the very top of the investigation pipeline, after automated and more expensive review stages.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a thing I think about a lot, and the core problem is a numbers problem. If you're running, say, a million AI agents doing autonomous work inside your company, and each of them is taking thousands of actions a day, then even if only a tiny fraction of those actions look suspicious, you end up with way more flagged actions than any team of humans could ever look at. So you just can't have the process be "a human carefully reviews everything that trips a wire." That's dead on arrival.

So the way I think about it is as a kind of funnel. At the top you have cheap, automated classifiers looking at basically everything. These are going to be noisy, but that's fine, because their job isn't to make the final call, it's to throw away the overwhelming majority of stuff that's obviously benign. Then the things that get through go to more expensive automated review, maybe a trusted model that gets more context, that can look at the whole trajectory rather than a single action, and can ask "does this make sense given what the agent was supposed to be doing?" And then only the stuff that survives that gets to humans.

And I think the important thing at the human stage is that you're not really trying to adjudicate individual actions anymore. What you're trying to do is figure out whether there's a pattern. Because the scary scenario isn't "an agent did one weird thing." It's "the model has some tendency to do this kind of thing under these circumstances," and that's a fact about the model, not about the instance. So one really suspicious action that you can actually pin down is worth an enormous amount, because it tells you something about every copy of that model. That changes how you should spend your human attention: you want depth on a small number of cases rather than breadth.

The other piece I'd emphasize is that you should design the whole thing so that getting caught once is really bad for the AI, from the AI's perspective. If a scheming model has to take, say, a hundred risky actions over the course of a takeover attempt, and each one has even a few percent chance of being flagged and then genuinely investigated, that's a terrible bet for it. So you don't need to catch every bad action. You need to make it so that the expected cost of attempting anything is high, and that the investigation process, when it does fire, is actually capable of concluding "yes, this was a deliberate attempt," and then you act on that, you don't just shrug and reset the agent.

Where I think people go wrong is treating this like ordinary incident response, where you investigate things that caused damage. Here, most of the interesting cases won't have caused damage yet. So you need the investigation to be triggered by the intent you can infer, not by the outcome, and that's a pretty different muscle for organizations to build.

r001.rationale: The response describes cheap automated classifiers screening all actions, discarding the overwhelming majority, and passing the remaining flagged actions to more expensive automated review.

r002.rationale: It places humans at the end of the escalation funnel, reviewing only cases that survive automated screening and review.

astra-6.text:
I think you probably want a funnel. You’re going to have an enormous number of actions, and you can’t afford to have a human carefully investigate every one. So you need relatively cheap automated monitoring that flags things as suspicious, and then you spend progressively more effort on the things that look most concerning.

And the question at each stage shouldn’t just be, “Was this action bad?” It should also be, “What would we need to look at to figure out what was going on here?” Maybe you need more context about the task, or to inspect something the agent wrote, or to check whether its explanation actually matches what it did.

One important feature is that you don’t necessarily need to catch every dangerous action. If an AI has to make many attempts before it succeeds, catching one attempt might give you an opportunity to discover the broader problem and stop it. But that only helps if the investigation actually escalates when it finds evidence of something serious. If you just block that particular action and let the agent keep trying, you’ve potentially squandered the opportunity.

r001.rationale: The response describes cheap automated monitoring to flag suspicious actions, then progressively more effort on the most concerning ones, conveying that only a small, suspicious subset reaches expensive investigation.

r002.rationale: It describes escalating investigative effort but does not say that humans enter only relatively far along the hierarchy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you probably want a funnel. Your AI agents might take millions of actions, and you can’t investigate every one of those in detail. So you want relatively cheap monitoring that flags things that seem suspicious, and then you spend more effort investigating a much smaller number of cases.

And a key question is whether your investigation process would actually catch the AI doing something bad. It’s not enough to look at a bunch of flagged actions and conclude that they all seem fine. You want to test the whole process: have someone construct examples of an AI trying to get away with something, and see whether your monitors flag them and whether your investigators correctly figure out what happened.

You also want investigators to have enough context. An individual action might look innocuous, but be part of a sequence that’s clearly concerning. So the investigation needs to be able to expand from ‘Why did it run this command?’ to ‘What was it trying to accomplish, and what else has it done?’

r001.rationale: The response proposes cheap monitoring that flags suspicious actions for more intensive investigation of a much smaller number of cases, but it does not say that the monitor is AI or that it selects the most suspicious AI-proposed actions.

r002.rationale: The response describes escalating effort and mentions investigators, but does not specify that humans enter only relatively far along an escalation hierarchy.
